Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . The American lobster, scientifically referred to as Homarus americanus, is the nearest relative of H. gammarus. Female H. gammarus attain sexual maturity when they reach a carapace length of 80 to 85 millimeters (3.1 to 3.3 inches), while males mature at a marginally smaller size. The eggs hatch during the night, prompting the larvae to swim toward the water's surface, where they are swept along by ocean currents while feeding on zooplankton. Homarus gammarus is located in the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway to the Azores and Morocco, but it is absent from the Baltic Sea. This species is widespread throughout much of the Mediterranean Sea, with the exception of the region to the east of Crete, and it is restricted to the northwestern shoreline of the Black Sea. The northernmost populations can be found in the Norwegian fjords, which fall within the Arctic Circle.

This specimen was collected from a location at 57° 53′ N 11° 32′ E, near Marstrand, Sweden, roughly 48 kilometers (30 miles) northwest of Gothenburg. Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976) was a high-ranking official in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). Raised in Tasmania, he enrolled as an air cadet in the RAAF in January 1934. Prior to World War II, he focused on enhancing his flight training and navigation abilities. In April 1941, he took command of No. 2 Squadron, which operated Lockheed Hudson aircraft. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December, engaging in combat against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. After returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam took on various staff and training positions, ultimately concluding the war with the rank of group captain.

In 1946, Headlam held the position of Officer Commanding for the North Western Area, and from 1947 to 1950, he served as the Director of Training. During the Malayan Emergency, which lasted from 1950 to 1951, he was stationed in Singapore, where he commanded No. 90 (Composite) Wing and later RAF Tengah. Headlam was appointed Air Member for Personnel on two occasions, first in 1957 and then again from 1959 to 1960. He received the title of Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. After being promoted to air vice marshal, he occupied various important roles, including Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command from 1961 to 1962, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff from 1965 to 1966, and AOC Support Command from 1966 to 1967. In 1965, he was also honored as a Companion of the Order of the Bath. Following his tenure as head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam was born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania, to farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. He completed his education at <unk> College in Hobart in 1932. Despite his parents' objections, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. Frank received his flight training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) located at RAAF Point Cook in Victoria and was promoted to pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

After completing a conversion course, Headlam was posted to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. The official history of the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) before World War II mentions that the Seaplane Squadron operated with a limited fleet of aircraft and was part of No. 1 Flying Training School, utilizing planes such as Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, among others. During this time, Headlam was elevated to the rank of flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a paper on national defense, arguing that Australia could achieve near invulnerability through "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens remarked that this paper "effectively outlined the 'anti-lodgment' concept, which has remained a persistent aspect of RAAF strategic thinking."

In July 1936, Headlam completed a flying instructor course and subsequently joined No. 1 FTS. He was promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Beginning in July 1938, he participated in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, directed by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This program featured several prominent training flights that garnered extensive media attention, including an impressive twelve-day, 10,800-kilometre (6,700 mi) journey around Australia in November, where Headlam piloted one of three Avro Ansons. The following month, he commanded the three Ansons on a six-day mission over Central Australia. He excelled in the navigation course, receiving special acknowledgment for his accomplishments. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton in Victoria as a flight commander. He initially served with No. 2 Squadron before switching to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, with both squadrons operating Ansons.

After the onset of World War II, No. 1 Squadron engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance operations along Australia's southeastern coastline. Headlam served as a flight commander within the squadron until January 15, 1940, when he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton to assume the position of station navigation officer. On March 27, he became part of the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He was promoted to squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Just two weeks later, he wed Katherine Bridge at St Paul’s Anglican Church in Frankston, and they would later have a son and a daughter.

On April 15, 1941, Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron, which was based in Laverton, and was promoted to wing commander on July 1. The squadron, which was equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily carried out maritime patrols in southern waters until December 5, when four of its aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to concerns about potential Japanese aggression in the Pacific. On December 7, this group began operations at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the other eight Hudsons from No. 2 Squadron remained on standby in Darwin. The next day, after it was confirmed that Australia was officially at war in the Pacific, one of the Hudsons at Penfui targeted the Japanese vessel Nanyo Maru, which was suspected of being a radio ship, successfully grounding it. By December 12, Headlam had moved to Penfui, where he assumed the position of commanding officer for both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, the aircraft of No. 2 Squadron were stationed at Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The unit based in Penfui engaged in operations aimed at disrupting Japanese shipping linked to the Celebes invasion. On January 11, two Hudson bombers confronted three Japanese floatplanes attacking a transport vessel, successfully downing or damaging some enemy aircraft. However, the following day, both Hudsons were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. The Japanese conducted their first bombing raid on Penfui on January 26, 1942, leading to damage to multiple aircraft. Subsequently, the operational Hudsons were moved to Darwin, while Headlam and his crew stayed at Penfui to perform reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18, Headlam received orders to evacuate all personnel except for a small team to assist Sparrow Force in demolishing the airfield. He returned to Darwin the next day, coinciding with the city’s inaugural Japanese air raid. During this attack, four Hudsons from No. 2 Squadron were lost, necessitating the relocation of the remaining aircraft to Daly Waters, where they continued reconnaissance and bombing operations against Japanese forces in Timor.

Headlam held the position of Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command in Darwin until May 12, 1942. He was then reassigned to Nhill, Victoria, to serve as the commanding officer of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Ansons. In June, the staff from this school established No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School ( <unk> ), which also operated Ansons and was based in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He was elevated to group captain on December 1, 1943, and just eight days later, on December 9, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3 <unk>, which flew Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. After handing over command of No. 3 <unk>, he began his education at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. On January 12, 1945, he was appointed the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam was designated as the Officer Commanding of the North Western Area. By the end of that year, he was reassigned to Britain, where he attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and worked with the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. After returning to Australia in November 1947, he took on the role of Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, he succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as the leader of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, located at RAF Changi in Singapore. No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units engaged in the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, which operated Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, which flew Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns carried out area bombing in communist-held territories and targeted specific sites, while the Dakotas were responsible for courier services, transporting VIPs, conducting medical evacuations throughout Southeast Asia, airlifting troops and supplies, and distributing propaganda leaflets in Malaya. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a Dakota from No. 38 Squadron, which he was co-piloting during a supply drop, crash-landed in Kampong Aur, Pahang, due to an engine failure. In August 1951, he was appointed the commander of RAF Tengah in Singapore while still overseeing No. 90 Wing, which he officially handed over in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam took on the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command located in Penrith, New South Wales. During his time as SASO, the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) initiated the modernization of its fleet with the introduction of English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force also experienced a significant organizational overhaul, moving from a geography-based command-and-control structure to a functionally organized system. This transformation led to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. In October 1953, Eastern Area Command, which had effectively operated as an operational headquarters due to its management of various combat units, was restructured into Home Command. In recognition of his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam was awarded the title of Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was promoted to acting air commodore in May, and on October 7, 1954, it was announced that he would serve as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II.

On January 1, 1955, Headlam was elevated to the rank of substantive air commodore. In November of that same year, he was assigned to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and the following year, he began his studies at the Imperial Defence College. Upon his return to Australia, he took on the role of Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from March 19 to October 21, 1957, serving in an interim capacity between Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, between Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. In this position, Headlam participated in the Air Board, the governing body of the service comprised of senior officers and led by the Chief of the Air Staff. Additionally, he was one of two RAAF representatives on a committee chaired by businessman William John Allison, which assessed conditions for defense personnel; the committee's recommendations resulted in a substantial increase in flight pay, among other enhancements. Furthermore, Headlam held various roles within the Department of Air, including Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, the latter position putting him in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. He was honored as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) during the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours, which were announced on June 3. In May 1960, he took on the role of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam became a member of the Operational Command (OPCOM) team, which had assumed responsibilities from Home Command to oversee RAAF operational units. In April, he succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as the Air Officer Commanding (AOC) of OPCOM. He achieved the rank of air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, he was assigned to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, and just a week later, he began his role as the AOC for No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch took over from him as AOC OPCOM. During his time as AOC for No. 224 Group, Headlam managed regional air defense and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962, followed by the onset of the Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which officially began the next month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he married the widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. He handed over command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Upon his return to Australia, Headlam took on the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on 26 January 1965. He was awarded the title of Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on 22 June in recognition of his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His time as DCAS coincided with the Air Force's largest rearmament initiative since World War II, a task complicated by staffing shortages stemming from the expansion and Australia's growing security commitments in Southeast Asia. Towards the end of his term, the first RAAF helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War; in March 1966, he visited Saigon alongside Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to strategize deployment plans. A year earlier, Wilton had suggested to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, sending two Iroquois helicopters to Vietnam for training purposes, but this proposal was declined by Murdoch, leaving the RAAF helicopter squadron unprepared for its collaborative function with the army upon its arrival. On 8 August 1966, Headlam replaced Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as the Air Officer Commanding Support Command in Melbourne, which had been established in 1959 through the merger of the RAAF’s previous Training and Maintenance Commands. He was later appointed as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London on 1 January 1968. Additionally, he served as Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971.

Upon his return to Australia in June 1971, Headlam took a period for adjustment before officially retiring from the Air Force on August 3. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a lengthy struggle with cancer. He is remembered by his children and his second wife. A private funeral service was held, and he was cremated at the Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 serves as a vital trunkline in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, connecting Fremont to Howard City. The stretch between Newaygo and Howard City passes through Fremont and runs along the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. This iteration of M-82 is the second in the state's history; the original was created in the Upper Peninsula around 1919. The route in the Lower Peninsula has largely remained unchanged since the 1920s, although there have been various extensions and reductions that have moved the western terminus to locations such as New Era or Hesperia. The current alignment was established in the late 1970s.

M @-@ 82 starts at a junction with M @-@ 120 and B @-@ 96, located to the west of Fremont. This intersection marks the convergence of three county lines. M @-@ 120 serves as the north-south boundary separating Newaygo and Oceana counties, as well as Newaygo and Muskegon counties. On the other hand, B @-@ 96 delineates the east-west boundary for Oceana and Muskegon counties, extending directly west from this point. From here, M @-@ 82 proceeds east along 48th Street, moving through agricultural areas until it arrives in Fremont. Upon entering the town, it changes into Main Street, passing through the downtown district before M @-@ 82 turns south onto Stewart Avenue as it leaves the city. The highway then curves onto 72nd Street, continuing east through additional farming areas. As M @-@ 82 approaches Newaygo, the landscape becomes more forested near the Muskegon River. The route follows Fremont Street until it intersects with M @-@ 37. The two highways merge, crossing the river and entering downtown along State Street. Just south of downtown, M @-@ 82 turns east once more, separating from M @-@ 37 and following 82nd Street along the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern terminus of M @-@ 82 is located at exit 118 on US 131 / M @-@ 46, west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) oversees the upkeep of its roadways and consistently tracks traffic trends. This tracking utilizes a measurement called average annual daily traffic (AADT), which reflects the typical number of vehicles that travel on a given road segment each day throughout the year. In 2009, MDOT observed that the peak traffic volume on M-82, situated west of Fremont, hit 16,532 vehicles per day. Conversely, the lowest volume recorded was 4,018 vehicles to the east of Newaygo. Furthermore, MDOT has not designated any portion of this highway as part of the National Highway System, which comprises roads crucial to the nation’s economy, defense, and transportation infrastructure.

The current M-82 was established in 1926, extending from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. This route passed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking the place of the earlier M-41 alignment. In late 1936, M-46 was expanded to link Newaygo with Howard City, creating a concurrency with M-82 to close a gap in the M-46 path. By 1938, this shared portion was designated solely as M-46, which returned M-82 to its northern connection with M-37 in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was re-routed along a new path west of Ferry, changing its direction from northwest towards Hart to a westward endpoint in Shelby.

In 1963 and 1964, the western segment of the highway underwent two realignments, extending from Hesperia to New Era while bypassing Ferry. A significant modification occurred around 1969, resulting in a restructuring of highway designations in Oceana County. M-20 took over M-82 west of Hesperia, ending at New Era instead of Muskegon. At the same time, M-120 began managing the section south of Hesperia, and M-82 became limited to the route connecting Hesperia and Newaygo. In 1973, the highway's length was extended as the eastern terminus was repositioned to Howard City. M-46 was redirected to link the US 131 freeway from Howard City to Cedar Springs, taking over M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This reorganization allowed the segment from Newaygo to Howard City to revert to the M-82 designation. The final change occurred in 1978, when the overlap with M-120 was removed in favor of M-120, resulting in the M-82 designation being confined to the junction west of Fremont, thus completing the current route of the highway.

Shikamaru Nara (Nara Shikamaru) is a character from the Naruto manga and anime series created by Masashi Kishimoto. Furthermore, the narrative delves into Shikamaru’s evolving relationship with Temari, highlighting his dilemma in deciding on their child's name, which occurs years after the primary storyline.

Shikamaru has consistently performed well in the popularity polls of Weekly Shōnen Jump, frequently landing in the top ten and achieving a notable fourth place at least once. In the most recent poll conducted in 2011, he finished in ninth place, situated between Sasori and Hinata. A wide range of merchandise featuring Shikamaru has been produced, such as action figures, keychains, and patches that showcase his character from both Part I and Part II. Additionally, NTT customers have ranked him as the sixteenth most popular black-haired male anime character. Hiroshi Matsuyama, the CEO of CyberConnect2, has expressed that Shikamaru is among his favorite characters from Naruto.

Many articles have examined Shikamaru's character in manga, anime, video games, and related media. IGN recognized him as one of the series' top characters, referring to him as "the poster child for any card-carrying member of Generation X" because of his notable apathy and reluctance to embrace his full potential. In their review of episode 110, IGN commended Shikamaru for overcoming his laid-back nature and stepping up as a leader during the mission to save Sasuke Uchiha, agreeing that his promotion to Chunin was well-earned. Anime News Network also acknowledged this transformation, describing Shikamaru's growth into "an unlikely hero" as a key highlight of the arc. In a later review of episode 135, which depicted the unsuccessful attempt to rescue Sasuke and the serious injuries sustained by Shikamaru's team, IGN pointed out the "great moment" when Shikamaru cried upon learning that his friends would recover, emphasizing his development into a more competent leader for them. Justin Rich from Mania Entertainment praised Shikamaru's "sheer intellect," labeling him "one of the most fascinating characters in the series" and "one of the few truly brilliant fighters in shōnen anime." Dani Moure, another reviewer from the same outlet, noted Shikamaru's battle with Temari during the Chunin Exams as "one of the better contests involving supporting characters."

Meridian is the sixth largest city in Mississippi, USA, and serves as the county seat for Lauderdale County. It is the primary city in the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. The city is conveniently located along key highways, positioned 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860 at the crossroads of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian's economy expanded alongside the railroads and the goods they carried, establishing it as a significant commercial hub. In February 1864, during the American Civil War, General William Tecumseh Sherman set fire to a considerable area of the city during the Battle of Meridian.

After the war, the city underwent a reconstruction phase and entered what is known as a "Golden Age." During this time, from 1890 to 1930, it became the largest city in Mississippi and evolved into a key manufacturing hub in the South, with 44 trains operating daily. Union Station, which opened in 1906, now serves as a multi-modal transportation center, linking to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, accommodating approximately 242,360 passengers annually. Despite facing economic difficulties due to a downturn in the railroad industry, the city successfully diversified its economy, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors dominating employment by 2010. According to the 2008 census, the estimated population within the city limits was 38,232, while the total population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius was 232,900, and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius. Additionally, 104,600 and 234,200 individuals respectively made up the labor force, contributing significantly to the city's economic vitality.

The region is bolstered by two military installations: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which collectively offer more than 4,000 employment opportunities. NAS Meridian hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and is notable for being the first Department of Homeland Security office established in the state. Key Field is named in honor of brothers Fred and Al Key, who set a world endurance flight record in 1935. Currently, the field is home to the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and functions as a base for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the largest non-military employer in the area, providing jobs for 2,610 individuals.

The city boasts a diverse array of cultural institutions and historical landmarks, including the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Meridian once housed two Carnegie libraries that catered to both the white and African American communities. The Carnegie Branch Library, which has since been demolished, was among a number of Carnegie libraries established for African Americans in the Southern United States during the segregation period.

The city has been chosen to host the future Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. Jimmie Rodgers, known as the "Father of Country Music," was born in Meridian. Within Highland Park, there exists a museum that celebrates his life and career, showcasing memorabilia and artifacts from the steam engine era. The park also features the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, which is recognized as a National Historic Landmark and is the last remaining two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. Notable individuals from the area include Susan Akin, Miss America 1986; James Chaney, an activist who was murdered during the Mississippi civil rights movement in 1964; and Hartley Peavey, the founder of Peavey Electronics, which is based in Meridian. The federal courthouse hosted the trial from 1966 to 1967 for those charged in the killings of Chaney and two other activists; this trial was significant as it marked the first instance in which a white jury convicted a white official for a murder associated with civil rights.

The region now known as Meridian was first occupied by the Choctaw Native Americans and came under U.S. jurisdiction with the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, amid the era of Indian Removal. Following the ratification of the treaty, European American settlers began to migrate into the area.

After obtaining a federal land grant of approximately 2,000 acres (810 hectares), Richard McLemore, the initial settler of Meridian, began providing free land to attract new residents and stimulate growth in the area. In 1853, Lewis A. Ragsdale, a lawyer hailing from Alabama, acquired the majority of McLemore's land. The remaining 80 acres (0.32 km²) were bought by John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County. Recognized as the founders of the city, Ragsdale and Ball commenced the subdivision of their respective tracts into lots for future development.

A significant dispute emerged regarding the name of the settlement. Ball and the local industrial residents favored "Meridian," associating it with "junction." In contrast, the farming community supported the name "<unk>" (which translates to "mad river" in a Native American language), inspired by a nearby stream. Ragsdale suggested naming it "Ragsdale City." To promote this name, Ball constructed a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, where a sign alternated each day between "Meridian" and "<unk>." Ultimately, the swift expansion of the railroads drew a large influx of railroad workers, who outnumbered other residents and established "Meridian" as the official name of the station. The town was officially incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

At the outset of the American Civil War in 1861, Meridian was merely a small community. Its advantageous location at a railroad junction prompted the Confederacy to establish several military installations to support their war efforts. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman led his troops into the town, demolishing the railroads in every direction, as well as an arsenal and extensive storage facilities; a significant part of the town's infrastructure was set ablaze. Sherman is said to have remarked afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." Nevertheless, the city's railroad lines were swiftly restored, and operations resumed within just 26 working days following the battle. Throughout the Reconstruction era, racial tensions persisted, exemplified by the riot in 1871 that erupted after a fire damaged several businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town experienced significant growth and entered a thriving period referred to as its "Golden Age" between 1880 and 1910. The introduction of railroads enhanced transportation and attracted various industries, leading to a surge in population. As the number of residents increased, commercial activities thrived in the downtown area. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian emerged as the largest city in Mississippi and a key manufacturing hub in the South. Numerous prominent historical structures were constructed during this era and shortly thereafter, including the Grand Opera House, which opened in 1890, the Wechsler School founded in 1894, two Carnegie libraries established in 1913, and the <unk> Building, completed in 1929, which became Meridian's tallest skyscraper.

The city experienced remarkable expansion, driven by a commission government that aimed to establish 90 new industrial sites in 1913, along with a thriving automobile sector in the 1920s. Even in the face of the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression, the city managed to attract new businesses. Amid the hardships of the Depression, the S. H. Kress & Co. building was opened in downtown Meridian, designed to "provide luxury to the average person," alongside the Temple Theater, which functioned as a cinema. Additionally, the federal courthouse was constructed in 1933 as part of a WPA initiative.

Following a short economic slump at the end of the Depression, the nation entered World War II, which reinvigorated the significance of railroads. Railways were crucial in transporting gasoline and scrap metal essential for the production of military vehicles, aiding in the resurgence of Meridian as the railway hub of the area. This economic growth persisted until the 1950s, when automobiles and the Interstate Highway System started to overshadow passenger trains. The downturn in the railroad sector resulted in considerable job losses, prompting many workers to move away, leading to a decline in population.

During the 1960s, in the midst of the American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian became a hub for the Council of Federated Organizations (CFO) and numerous other activist groups. Local activists like James Chaney, along with Michael <unk>, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman—who were volunteers from the North—aimed to establish a community center that offered classes to empower African Americans in the region to reclaim their voting rights. This activism incited anger among local white residents, often leading to violent confrontations as racial tensions escalated. In June 1964, Chaney, <unk>, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to meet with members of a black church that had experienced a bombing and arson. That evening, while returning to Meridian, the three disappeared. After an extensive investigation by the FBI, their bodies were discovered two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

In a federal courthouse located in Meridian, seven members of the Ku Klux Klan, including a deputy sheriff, were convicted of "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while three others were acquitted in a trial concerning the murders of civil rights activists in Mississippi. This case marked the first instance where a white jury convicted "a white official in a civil rights homicide." In 2005, the state reopened the investigation, leading to charges being filed for the first time. Edgar Ray Killen was found guilty of manslaughter and sentenced to 60 years behind bars. In memory of Chaney, a section of 49th Avenue in Meridian was renamed in his honor, and an annual memorial service was initiated.

Beginning in the 1960s, the growth of highways facilitated commuting, encouraging people to relocate from the downtown area to newly developed residential neighborhoods in the north. As strip malls started to encroach upon the city center, the city took action in the 1970s and 1980s by establishing multiple zones as historic districts to safeguard its architectural legacy. In 1979, the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was created, followed by the launch of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street initiated several projects aimed at revitalizing the downtown area, which included the establishment of a new Amtrak Station in 1997, drawing inspiration from the former train station that had once served the city during its heyday before its demolition. Additional efforts comprised the restoration of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside the promotion of a unified urban design. In collaboration with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street played a key role in the renovation of the historic Grand Opera House in 2006, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of Meridian Main Street's ownership to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, both entities, along with the Meridian Downtown Association, embarked on efforts to rejuvenate the downtown area. The Alliance acts as a pivotal organization, providing staff support and resources to the other two groups while facilitating communication between them. Despite intentions to renovate the <unk> Building, newly appointed Mayor Cheri Barry paused those plans in early 2010. At present, the Alliance is focused on promoting further growth and revitalization in downtown, particularly by supporting businesses like specialty shops, restaurants, and bars that contribute to a lively atmosphere both day and night. Simultaneously, the Meridian Downtown Association is striving to boost foot traffic through the organization of special events, while the Meridian Main Street program seeks to aid local businesses in the community.

Meridian's position as a railway hub has led to the establishment of various hotels catering to travelers. Even prior to Meridian's "Golden Age," several significant hotels, such as the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue, were founded before the 20th century. The expansion of railroads and the inauguration of the original Union Station in 1906 prompted the development of additional hotels to serve passengers and workers alike. The Elmira Hotel was built in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian opened its doors in 1907, and the Union Hotel was founded in 1908. In 1979, the Union Hotel earned a spot on the National Register of Historic Places, while both Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were recognized as key sites in the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, its hotels showcased the aspirations of a prosperous economy, particularly highlighted by the Lamar Hotel, an eleven-story building that was finished in 1927. This hotel was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and later transformed into a county annex facility. In 1988, it received recognition as a Mississippi Landmark.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel emerged as a significant venue within the African American business area that formed to the west of downtown. During the era of segregation, it was notable for being one of the few locations in the city that offered accommodations to African American travelers.

During the 1960s and 1970s, the expansion of suburban regions led to a trend of hotels relocating from urban centers. The renovation of the Riley Center in 2006 heightened the demand for a new hotel in the downtown locale. A proposal was made to transform the <unk> Building into a hotel, but the renovation encountered obstacles due to shifts in city leadership. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was established to boost public awareness and support for the building's restoration, providing first-floor tours and coordinating anniversary celebrations.

The Meridian Downtown Historic District combines two prior districts: the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. Since 1985, Meridian has functioned under a "strong mayor" governance model, characterized by a mayor-council system. The mayor, elected by the entire electorate every four years, serves as the city's chief executive officer, overseeing and directing the daily operations of the city government. Additionally, five city council members are elected every four years, with each one representing one of the five wards, designated as single-member districts. Meanwhile, the city council serves as the legislative body, tasked with formulating policies and sanctioning the city's annual budget.

City Hall, which is on the National Register of Historic Places, can be found at 601 23rd Avenue. Percy Bland is the current mayor. The city council consists of Dr. George M. Thomas representing Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson for Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon of Ward 5. Pam McInnis serves as the clerk of the council. The city employs a total of 570 individuals.

Following the devastation of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city created a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), distinguishing it as the only local DHS in the state. This department is responsible for an area that includes nine counties. With $2.5 million in funding secured from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other entities, the department initiated training programs for law enforcement personnel from nearby Southern states in passenger rail rescue methods, in addition to providing civilian courses in basic handgun skills, first aid for Boy Scouts, hunting, and firearm safety. The DHS proves vital during crises, as evidenced during Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it assisted in establishing and managing shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which is comprised of three teams, each serving nine counties.

Since 2009, the Meridian Police Department, under the leadership of Police Chief Lee <unk>, has comprised 115 full-time officers, along with part-time and reserve personnel. That same year, the Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, with 2,000 of those classified as felonies. Crime data from 2009 indicated a slight increase compared to the prior year. Meridian is acknowledged as "the safest city in Mississippi with a population exceeding 30,000." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, located in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian, is managed by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections. Furthermore, the Meridian Fire Department, led by Chief Anthony Clayton, responded to over 1,600 calls in 2009, which included 123 incidents of structural fires and 609 emergency service calls.

In the realm of state politics, the Senate district map for Mississippi delineates the city into three distinct zones. The northernmost zone is part of the 31st State Senate District, represented by Terry Clark Burton (R). A stretch from the southwest to the northeast corner of the city is included in the 32nd State Senate District, with Sampson Jackson, II (D) serving as its representative. Meanwhile, the western and southeastern parts of the city are encompassed by the 33rd State Senate District, represented by <unk> Carmichael (R). In terms of the Mississippi House of Representatives, the city is divided into four districts. The southern and eastern regions fall within House District 81, represented by Steven A. Horne (R). The central area of the city encompasses all of House District 82, represented by Wilbert L. Jones (D). Surrounding House District 82 is House District 83, represented by Greg Snowden (R). Lastly, the western part of the city, along with a small northern section, is included in House District 84, represented by Tad Campbell (R).

At the national level, the city falls within Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, currently represented by Gregg Harper (R), who has held the position since 2009. Meridian is located in Lauderdale County, which has consistently backed the Republican candidate in every U.S. presidential election since 1972. Before this trend towards Republican support, the white electorate in the area predominantly leaned towards Democratic candidates, as the region was largely influenced by a single political party for many decades following the late 19th century.

The development of the city has mirrored the influence of various social and economic dynamics. From its establishment until 1970, the population consistently increased with each census, although the rates of growth fluctuated significantly, reaching a high of 165% and dropping to just 0.2%. The census in 1970 indicated a decline in population; however, by 1980, there was a slight uptick, which was then followed by a continuous decrease until the early 21st century when growth resumed. Between 1980 and 2000, the population decreased by over 14%. The census in 2000 recorded a population of 39,968, resulting in a density of 885.9 residents per square mile (342.0/km²). By 2008, the city had grown to be the sixth largest in the state, and an increase in population was noted in 2010.

Meridian serves as the central city of the Meridian region, which, as of 2009, included three counties: Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale, with a combined population of 106,139. The population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius is 232,900, and it rises to 526,500 when extending the radius to 65 miles (105 km).

Although the city's total population has seen variations, there has been a consistent increase in both the number and proportion of non-white residents. The only decrease in this group occurred between 1960 and 1970, a period marked by a significant drop in the city’s overall population. According to the 2010 Census, the city's racial composition was 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.09% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other racial backgrounds, and 0.89% identifying as belonging to two or more races. Furthermore, individuals identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race constituted 1.75% of the population.

As reported by the 2000 Census, the city contained a total of 17,890 housing units, with 15,966 of those being occupied; among the occupied units, there were 10,033 family homes. Of the occupied residences, 31.1% had children under 18 years old, 36.2% were comprised of married couples, 23.3% were led by female householders without a spouse, and 37.2% fell into the category of non-family households. Individuals made up 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% included at least one person aged 65 or older living alone. The average size of a household was 2.39, while family households had an average of 3.06 members. Since 1970, the average household size has consistently decreased from 3.04. Additionally, the median age in Meridian rose from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 by 2000.

The median income for households in the city stood at $25,085, while the median income for families was $31,062. Males earned a median income of $29,404, compared to females, who had a median income of $19,702. The city's per capita income was noted to be $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the overall population were living below the poverty line, which included 40.8% of individuals under 18 years old and 22.0% of those aged 65 and older.

The population of Meridian and its surrounding areas exhibits significant religious involvement, with 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents reporting membership in a religious organization, surpassing the national average of 50.2%. In the year 2000, among those who identified with a religion, 30,068 individuals (59.0%) were linked to the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 (18.6%) were affiliated with the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 (3.7%) were associated with the Catholic Church.

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe played a crucial role in the economic growth of the city by establishing a variety of businesses and services. The Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, shortly before the city's "Golden Age." By 1927, Meridian boasted the largest Jewish population in the state, totaling 575 members. In contrast, today there are fewer than 40 Jews residing in Meridian, the majority of whom are elderly.

Meridian is situated in the North Central Hills region of Mississippi, specifically in Lauderdale County. According to the United States Census Bureau, the city spans an area of 45.9 square miles (119 km²), which consists of 45.1 square miles (117 km²) of land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) of water. In terms of major highways, Meridian is located 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The surrounding area is characterized by cotton and corn fields, as well as oak and pine forests, forming a landscape of clay hills and lower regions near the headwaters of an unnamed river.

The city's urban core has altered its natural landscape by leveling it, yet the surrounding regions continue to display softly undulating hills. Scattered throughout the city, especially in the northern and southern sections, are numerous small streams, lakes, and wooded areas. In the southern region, <unk> Creek flows and divides into Gallagher's Creek, which traverses the city's center. Loper's Creek is located in the far west, along with several smaller streams such as Shearer’s Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek found throughout the city.

Meridian is situated in a region characterized by a humid subtropical climate. Throughout the summer months, specifically from June to August, the average high temperature hovers around 90 °F (32 °C), while the typical low is about 70 °F (21 °C). Conversely, during the winter season, from December to February, the average high temperature drops to roughly 60 °F (16 °C), and the average low decreases to around 35 °F (2 °C). Typically, July is the hottest month, registering an average high of 92.9 °F (33.8 °C), whereas January is noted as the coldest month, with an average low of 34.7 °F (1.5 °C).

The city sees an average annual rainfall of 58.65 inches (1,490 mm). Precipitation is relatively consistent throughout the year, with March being the wettest month, averaging 6.93 inches (176 mm). A significant share of this rainfall results from thunderstorms, which are prevalent during the summer but can happen year-round. Severe thunderstorms can lead to destructive winds and large hail, in addition to the typical hazards posed by lightning and heavy rain. These extreme weather events are most frequently noted in the spring, with another increase in occurrences during the fall. Additionally, these storms can potentially produce tornadoes.

During its early development, the economy heavily relied on the railroads in the area. By the early 1900s, the city had become the largest in Mississippi, featuring five major rail lines and 44 trains running each day. The local economy was closely tied not only to the railroads but also to the goods they transported, including timber and cotton. From approximately 1890 to 1930, these railroad-dependent sectors were essential in positioning the city as a significant economic hub within the state and surrounding areas. Although the city encountered economic difficulties due to a decline in the railroad industry during the 1950s, it successfully transitioned from a railroad-focused economy to a more diversified one, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing now representing the majority of job opportunities.

Meridian, along with Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, benefits from the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established by local entrepreneurs in 1996. By April 2010, the city's civilian labor force reached 15,420, with a population of 232,900 in a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, leading to labor force estimates of 104,600 and 234,200, respectively. Consequently, the city acts as a center for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities. Eighty percent of Lauderdale County's workforce lives within the county, while 90% reside within 45 miles.

As of April 2010, the healthcare sector in Lauderdale County employed a total of 6,260 individuals. The leading healthcare provider in the area is Rush Hospital, which has 2,610 employees, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital with 1,500 workers and Anderson Hospital, employing 1,475. Meridian is home to three hospitals along with several other healthcare facilities. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center provides services including cardiovascular surgery, a Level II neonatal intensive care unit, and a health and fitness center. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital, in collaboration with Rush Health Systems, manages the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, which specializes in long-term care for patients needing extended recovery in a hospital environment. Riley Hospital features two centers focused on stroke treatment and rehabilitation services. Other healthcare institutions in Meridian include the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, a community resource that has been serving the area since 1882.

The retail industry is vital for employment in the county, employing 5,280 individuals as of April 2010. Annually, approximately $2 billion is allocated to retail expenditures within the city. Bonita Lakes Mall encompasses 633,685 square feet (58,871 m²) and features over one hundred shopping options, including department stores, specialty retailers, dining establishments, and United Artists Theatres. The first phase of the Meridian Crossroads shopping center, which covers 375,000 square feet (34,800 m²) in the Bonita Lakes area, was completed in November 2007, significantly enhancing the local retail landscape. Additionally, the shopping district on North Hills Street has been growing, with new retail and office spaces launching in March 2007 near the Walmart Supercenter on Highway 19.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which collectively generate more than 4,000 job opportunities for the local community. NAS Meridian is responsible for training naval carrier pilots and various enlisted personnel, and it also houses the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCDTA), which offers drug enforcement training to law enforcement bodies across several southeastern states. The city is proud to host the state's inaugural local Department of Homeland Security and plays a significant role as a leader for a nine-county regional response team, in addition to a twenty-nine county regional response task force. Key Field holds historical importance due to the record-setting endurance flight achieved by brothers Fred and Al Key in 1935. Currently, Key Field is home to the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and acts as a support facility for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. Moreover, the site features an exhibit dedicated to aviation history and is home to Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, the manufacturing industry in Lauderdale County provided jobs for 2,850 individuals. Peavey Electronics Corporation, founded in 1965, has been producing guitars, amplifiers, and audio equipment in the city. Additionally, other prominent companies in the region include Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. The city also features four industrial parks.

Located in the heart of downtown, the MSU Riley Center not only promotes tourism but also supports the arts and entertainment scene. Each year, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian for various conferences, meetings, and performances. Meanwhile, Loeb's Department Store on Front Street has been a leading clothing retailer in Mississippi, staying within family ownership for four generations. Established by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has a longstanding reputation for offering quality apparel for both men and women.

Meridian is home to a vibrant artistic legacy that has flourished for over a century, hosting a variety of cultural organizations and events. The Meridian Art League, founded in February 1933, is one of the city's earliest art institutions. Initially, art shows took place at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian, but in 1949, the group was renamed the Meridian Art Association and began exhibiting in multiple venues across the city. After the closure of the Carnegie Library at the intersection of 25th Ave and 7th St, the Art Association transformed the former library space into the Meridian Museum of Art, establishing a dedicated location for its displays. The museum opened its doors in 1970 and has since presented a diverse range of exhibitions, alongside extensive educational programs for both adults and students. Annually, the museum hosts over thirty exhibitions that showcase a wide array of artworks, including traditional decorative arts, ethnographic and tribal pieces, photography, crafts, and more. Its collection features portraits from the 18th and 19th centuries, photography from the 20th century, and various sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) was established in 1978 as the official arts organization for Meridian and Lauderdale County. MCA manages the Community Art Grants program, coordinates the annual <unk> Festival, offers a variety of workshops, and organizes numerous special events throughout the year. The council collaborates with several local arts organizations, including the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, recognized as one of the oldest subscription community theaters in the Southern U.S., was constructed in 1932 and attracts over 22,000 visitors each season, making it Mississippi's most popular community theater. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra (<unk>), founded in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and began its first full season in 1963. In 1965, the <unk> featured its first international soloist, Elena <unk>, who performed alongside the orchestra. Additionally, the Orchestra has supported the Meridian Public School District in establishing its own orchestra and strings programs, as well as helped create the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, who has been conducting since 1991, currently leads the orchestra, which is set to celebrate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

Established in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, the Grand Opera House has a rich history of showcasing various renowned artists and performances, starting with a German company’s production of Johann Strauss II’s "The Gypsy Baron." Unfortunately, the opera house closed in the late 1920s as a result of the Great Depression and remained neglected for almost seventy years. In 2000, a major restoration effort began, supported by a $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation, established in 1998, along with an additional $15 million from various city, county, and federal sources. The renovation was finalized in September 2006, at which point the venue was renamed the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center features a 950-seat auditorium for live events, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting space, drawing over 60,000 visitors annually to downtown Meridian for conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is rightly celebrated as an architectural gem, recognized as one of the best-preserved early 20th-century cities in the United States. The public education system in Meridian was initiated under the Mississippi Constitution of 1870. Meridian is home to the Meridian Lauderdale County Public Library, located at the intersection of 7th Street and 26th Avenue. "Angel of Death" serves as the opening track on Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood, by the American thrash metal band. The song's lyrics and composition were crafted by Slayer's guitarist, Jeff Hanneman, who drew inspiration from Josef Mengele, a notorious Nazi doctor known for his inhumane experiments at Auschwitz during World War II. Consequently, the band has encountered multiple allegations of Nazi sympathies and racism over the course of their career.

Although there have been conversations about the song and its influence on postponing the release of Reign in Blood, "Angel of Death" is featured in all of Slayer's live albums and DVDs, and it has been highlighted in multiple films. The song has been praised by critics, with Steve Huey from AllMusic calling it a "classic."

Jeff Hanneman, Slayer's guitarist, composed "Angel of Death" after delving into literature regarding Nazi physician Josef Mengele during the band's tour. He recalled, "I remember pausing at a location where I purchased two books about Mengele. I thought to myself, 'This must have some dark content.' Consequently, when it was time to focus on the album, those concepts were fresh in my mind — that’s what influenced the lyrics of 'Angel of Death.'"

The lyrics describe the surgical experiments performed by Mengele on inmates at Auschwitz during World War II. His studies targeted specific groups, particularly dwarfs and twins, and included both physical and psychological assessments. The song "Angel of Death" references various procedures he undertook, including surgeries done without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, confinement for endurance trials, gassing, injections of lethal pathogens, sex reassignment surgeries, and the removal of organs and limbs, among other methods.

"Joining their efforts, but it's merely a matter of time before conflicts arise," is a phrase from the penultimate verse that alludes to allegations against Mengele concerning his experiments on twins, including one with a physical deformity. Reports indicate that "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back, with their wrists also attached." This claim was initially revealed by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, who is referred to as the "architect of the Holocaust." It was alleged that Mengele "linked their veins" and transformed them into conjoined twins. This accusation gained further prominence after Vera Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary The Search for Mengele, which has been referenced by numerous authors, including Gerald Posner, a noted expert on Mengele.

The lyrics of "Angel of Death" played a major role in postponing the release of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. Even though they had a deal with Def Jam Records, their distributor Columbia Records declined to put out the album, citing concerns over its lyrical themes and cover art, which they considered "too graphic." Ultimately, Reign in Blood was released by Geffen Records on October 7, 1986. However, because of the ensuing controversy, the album was excluded from Geffen Records' official release catalog.
